samples.text:
The table shows the percentage of households in one country which had five different household appliances in 1970, 1990, 2010 and 2020.

In 1970, refrigerator and washing machine was the most common appliances, with 58% and 64% of households. Very few households had a dishwasher (3%) or a tumble dryer (1%), and nobody had a microwave oven.

By 1990, the numbers went up a lot. Refrigerators increased to 96% and washing machines to 87%. Microwave ovens increase to 47% and tumble dryers to 45%, but dishwashers was still low with 14%.

In 2010 and 2020, refrigerators and washing machines was almost in every home, 99% and 97% in 2020. Microwave ovens also became very common, 92% in 2010 and 93% in 2020. Dishwashers rose to 40% and then 49%. However, tumble dryers went up to 57% in 2010 but after that it decreased a little to 55%.

Overall, the ownership of all appliances increased a lot over the period, and microwave oven had the biggest growth.
samples.why: Accurate figures organised chronologically · overview present but basic and placed last · repetitive trend language (went up, increased) · several agreement, tense and article errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The table illustrates the proportion of households in one country that owned a refrigerator, a washing machine, a dishwasher, a microwave oven and a tumble dryer at four points between 1970 and 2020.

Overall, ownership of all five appliances rose over the fifty-year period, although the pace of growth varied. Refrigerators and washing machines became almost universal, while microwave ovens experienced the most rapid increase. Dishwashers, however, remained the least common appliance.

In 1970, washing machines were the most widely owned appliance, found in 64% of homes, slightly more than refrigerators at 58%. Both became increasingly common over the following decades, and by 2020 virtually every household had a fridge (99%) and 97% had a washing machine.

Microwave ovens showed the most remarkable growth. Non-existent in homes in 1970, they were owned by 47% of households by 1990, 92% in 2010 and 93% in 2020. Tumble dryers also spread quickly at first, rising from just 1% to 45% by 1990 and 57% in 2010, but this figure fell slightly to 55% in the final year. Dishwashers grew more steadily, from 3% to 40% in 2010, and reached 49% in 2020, meaning that fewer than half of households own one.
samples.why: Clear overview of near-universal and slower-growing items · appliances grouped logically · good lexical range (non-existent, virtually) · mostly accurate grammar with a minor tense slip at the end.

samples.text:
The table charts the percentage of households in one country owning five household appliances in 1970, 1990, 2010 and 2020.

Ownership of every appliance was considerably higher in 2020 than in 1970, with the sharpest growth occurring between 1970 and 2010. By the end of the period, refrigerators, washing machines and microwave ovens were found in almost every home, whereas dishwashers and tumble dryers remained far less widespread.

Refrigerators and washing machines were already fairly common in 1970, owned by 58% and 64% of households respectively. Refrigerator ownership rose to 96% within twenty years and plateaued at 99% from 2010, while washing machines followed a more gradual path to 97%.

The microwave oven underwent the most dramatic transformation, from being absent from homes entirely in 1970 to featuring in almost half (47%) by 1990 and 93% by 2020. Tumble dryers were similarly rare at first, at 1%, and climbed to 57% in 2010, but they were the only appliance to decline thereafter, dipping to 55%. Dishwasher ownership, meanwhile, rose steadily from a mere 3% but still stood at just under half (49%) in the final year.
samples.why: Clear overview dividing common and less widespread appliances · key trends and the one reversal selected skilfully · cohesion effortless · precise vocabulary (plateaued, dipping) · wide range of accurate structures.
